newsitem.title: USA: Oregon electricity deregulation bill hits snags.
newsitem.headline: Oregon electricity deregulation bill hits snags.

text.p: As Oregon's legislative session draws toward its June 13 close, a bill to deregulate the state's power industry has taken shape.

But sources involved in crafting the legislation said Wednesday it has fallen short of satisfying either investor-owned or public utilities, who are questioning the way it deals with key issues like stranded cost and bonds.

"It is reasonably clear now the committee will come up with a bill. It is less clear whether it will have enough votes on the floor (to secure passage)," said John Larson, administrator of the Oregon House of Representative's Committee on Power Deregulation.

Denise McPhail, a lobbyist for Portland General Electric Co, said the utility and its future parent, Enron Corp, remain committed to competition, but believe the best option for Oregon would be further study of the issue.
At this stage, the bill is supported by large industrial electricity consumers and the Fair and Clean Energy Coalition, which represents small consumers and environmental groups.
The Eugene Water & Electric Board (EWEB), a public utility, has expressed informal support, but its board has not yet voted on it.
Investor-owned utilities, like Portland General (PGE) and PacifiCorp, object chiefly to terms for recovery of stranded costs, Larson said.
Under the bill, calculating utility costs deemed uneconomic under market competition would rest with the Oregon Public Utility Commission.
Enron Corp, which plans to acquire PGE later this year, is worried about recovery of costs such as PGE's investment in the cancelled Trojan nuclear plant, Larson said.
"The real upshot here is that Enron is opposed to deregulation for the first time ever," Larson noted.
While PGE lobbyist McPhail said the bill's schedule for competition is acceptable to the companies, she pointed out "it gives no direction whatsoever about stranded costs."
Under their merger application, PGE and Enron have pledged to file a restructuring plan for PGE's service territory, which represents 45 percent of the Oregon market.
"We are volunteering to be lab rats for Oregon," McPhail said.

Aside from EWEB, Oregon's public utilities are opposed to implementation of any restructuring legislation at this time, also preferring to carry out studies and pilot programs between now and the state's next legislative session, which is two years away, Larson said.
The public utilities are concerned about what will happen to their contracts to buy power from the federally managed Bonneville Power Administration after they expire October 1, 2001, he added.
The state's public utility districts are also worried about how the legislation will effect their tax-exempt bonds.
Under the proposed bill, Oregon's large industrial customers would be allowed to choose their power supplier as early as July 1, 1999, with the market open to all customers by 2001.
An earlier version of the bill would have allowed competition for all consumers by January 1, 2000.
Under the bill, utilities would dedicate three percent of total electricity revenues to the funding of conservation and and renewable energy programs starting January 1, 1999.
Larson said the committee will continue to work to come up with a final bill ahead of the session close, which may be extended into mid-July.
((--D Beasley, Los Angeles bureau + 1 213 955 6761))
